In the field of ML for engineering design, there is no comprehensive standardized set of benchmark problems and metrics for evaluating ML-based design methods. This paper introduces EngiBench, the first open-source library and datasets spanning diverse domains for data-driven engineering design. Various physics-based design problems (airfoils, heat/elasticity topology optimization, photonics, power-electronics, etc.) are included in EngiBench together with various ML methods. EngiBench also includes engineering-specific metrics such as cumulative optimality gap (COG), ratio of constraint violations (RVC), maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and determinantal point process (DPP) scores for diversity.

I think that the main strength of this paper is the diversity of the proposed EngiBench with respect the included problems, algorithms and metrics. EngiBench includes various challenging engineering problems (which are based on real physics simulators), various ML methods such as surrogate-based optimization, inverse design, and both conditional and unconditional generative models (like GANs, diffusion models, and BézierGANs), and various engineering-specific metrics.

Whereas some issues were pointed out by the reviewers, it seems that most of them have been addressed by the authors' rebuttal in a convincing manner. 

One issue is the accessibility for individual researchers without high-performance resources since distributed computing and high-fidelity simulations are mentioned in this paper. In the rebuttal, it is explained that some problems in EngiBench can be handled by lightweight Python-based simulations that run in seconds on a standard desktop or laptop whereas some other real-world application problems need high-performance computing.

Another issue is the diversity of problems. All problems are static and small scale problems with no dynamic multi-component tasks. In the rebuttal, it is explained that EngiBench welcomes external contributions, which will be explicitly mentioned in the final camera-read paper: "We will rename the appendix section “Maintenance” to “Maintenance and External Contributions” and explicitly link to our online guides for adding new problems or algorithms, which we are currently expanding."

Since the proposed EngiBench has high novelty and high comprehensibility with respect to the included problems, algorithms and metrics (as well as high evaluations by the reviewers: average score 4.75), I would like to recommend the acceptance of this paper.

Reviewer response to authors
Thank you for the thorough rebuttal and for clarifying several points.

For the camera-ready, please ensure the following items make it into the manuscript (not only the docs/repo):

A compact in-paper description of each baseline and any task-specific specializations with exact configs.
Dataset provenance and diversity definitions (how computed), plus parameter bounds and coverage for Airfoils.
A small table of typical solver failure modes and observed failure ratios per task.
Exact reproducibility details: commit hashes/tags, container images, seeds, and hardware/compute budgets.
Calibrated language around findings such as “GANs > diffusion” to emphasize task-specific and constraint-sensitive conditions.
These revisions will materially improve accessibility for ML readers and strengthen the empirical narrative, but since they are not yet reflected in the current submission, I will maintain my score at 4 (Borderline Accept) and confidence at 2. Reasons to accept still outweigh reasons to reject, especially given the breadth of tasks, unified API, and open-source availability.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for supporting our initiative. We indeed aim to provide a “Gym for engineering design” and hope the community will adopt it. We took care of the minor points which were mentioned, e.g., modified the optimization problem definition to be minimization instead of maximization, added a table-like notation for the order of the metrics in Table 2’s caption similar to $\frac{\text{COG} (\downarrow) \ | \text{RVC} (\downarrow)}{\text{MMD} (\downarrow) | \text{DPP} (\uparrow)}$ , and clarified that adjoint optimizers may be stuck in local optima. 

Below are our answers to the other concerns.

> The paper does not provide justification for the specific problems chosen. These problems do cover a number of domains, which is good, but some discussion could be added about the significance of the problems.

We selected the problems in Table 1 with the explicit goal of covering a broad spectrum of engineering design settings, different modeling modalities, and different costs/complexity/difficulty. In particular:
* **Representation diversity:** The problems span a range of design representations—from low-dimensional vectors (e.g., electronic parameters), to 2D images (e.g., pixel-based topology optimization), to 3D tensors (e.g., voxel-based topology optimization)—to reflect the heterogeneity of real-world design tasks.
* **Physics diversity:** The benchmark includes problems grounded in different physical domains such as fluid dynamics, structural elasticity, thermal diffusion, and power electronics, providing a robust testbed for general-purpose ML methods.
* **Objective diversity:** The selected problems include both single-objective and multi-objective settings.
* **Compute budget:** We include both computationally expensive problems (e.g., Airfoil optimization) and lightweight ones (e.g., Beams) to support both large-scale benchmarking and fast algorithm prototyping.
* **Benchmark alignment:** Several problems correspond to well-known benchmarks or existing in the literature. For example, our Airfoil, HeatConduction, and Beams2D problems are adapted from [1–4], making it easier for researchers to reproduce and extend prior work.

We will clarify these design choices in the revised paper next to Table 1. Thank you for the suggestion.





> ​​The benchmark problems seem to be quite specific in terms of actual configuration, and it would be nice to see more flexible configurations of these problems, for example in the heat conduction problem, one can imagine a user being able to specify multiple heat sources or sinks. Similarly multiple circuit configurations and topologies in the power electronics case would be a valuable addition. Adding some configuration options like this would mean that the problems would be representative of a larger range of real world problems.

We fully agree that allowing more customization would make the benchmark even more representative of real-world design settings. We’ve started exploring this direction with Beams2D, where users can already configure the applied force location and image resolution--we even provide different datasets for different resolutions (line 842). Similarly, in ongoing work (not yet part of EngiBench), we are investigating generalization for multiple converter topologies in PowerElectronics. However, as noted in Section 4.2, current models already struggle even under fixed configurations, which is why we chose to start with simplified settings to establish reliable baselines.

We will expand the discussion in the Use Cases, Limitations, and Future Work section to include this idea of parameterizable problem families, which we see as a natural evolution of the benchmark.

> One important aspect of a library like this is the possibility of users contributing new problems or more complex configurations of problems. As these contributions grow, so will the value of these benchmarks and this library. However extending the library with new problems doesn't seem to be discussed in the paper. I noticed there is some information about this in the documentation, though it may be good to include something in the paper on this point.

Thank you for the suggestion. Indeed, we briefly mention at line 621 that we welcome community contributions, but agree this could be made more visible. We will rename the appendix section “Maintenance” to “Maintenance and External Contributions” and explicitly link to our online guides for adding new problems or algorithms, which we are currently expanding.

> It looks like some of the datasets hosted on huggingface are quite small (almost all less than 5k examples, some with only 400). This is not necessarily a problem as one can relatively easily generate more data themselves, but it is always good to have more diversity in a dataset.

It is true that some of the datasets—particularly those for the heat conduction problem—are relatively small, with fewer than 5k examples. This is largely because these datasets originate from prior publications (e.g.,  [2, 3]), and are intended to support reproduction of those results. One of EngiBench’s goals is precisely to make such datasets accessible and reusable in a standardized format.

That said, we agree that increased dataset diversity and scale are valuable. Since EngiBench supports distributed compute (e.g., via our Slurm API), it is easy to generate larger datasets and publish new versions on HuggingFace.


## Bibliography
[1] Cashen Diniz and Mark Fuge. "Optimizing diffusion to diffuse optimal designs." In AIAA. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, 2024.

[2] Milad Habibi, Jun Wang, and Mark Fuge. "When is it actually worth learning inverse design?" In International Design Engineering Technical Conferences and Computers and Information in Engineering Conference, 2023.

[3] Milad Habibi, Shai Bernard, Jun Wang, and Mark Fuge. "Mean squared error may lead you astray when optimizing your inverse design methods." Journal of Mechanical Design, 2025.

[4] Erik Andreassen, Anders Clausen, Mattias Schevenels, Boyan S. Lazarov, and Ole Sigmund. "Efficient topology optimization in MATLAB using 88 lines of code." Structural and Multidisciplinary Optimization, 2011.

Thank you for your encouraging feedback. We also believe that standardized benchmarks in ML for engineering design are a very important topic for future research and are committed to making this field more accessible. We are glad the reviewer appreciates the benchmark breadth, our carefully designed API, and the experimental results. Below, we address the concerns written in the “Weaknesses” section of the review. 

> the discussion of the ML-based methods is still too thin.

We agree that the ML methods we present in the experiments were not discussed enough in the paper. We will add a concise section called "Implemented algorithms in EngiOpt," explaining that we provide well‑understood baselines (GANs, Diffusion, MLP+NSGA‑II) in single‑file implementations (CleanRL‑style), to maximize extensibility, debuggability, and reproducibility without heavy simulator‑specific dependencies. For the harder cases (i.e., Airfoil and PowerElectronics), we also include BézierGAN—a specialized model for Airfoils, and a stronger surrogate stack (robust preprocessing, Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimization, implicit ensembles, NSGA‑II) which has been experimentally validated in turbomachinery [1,2]. Despite these specializations, these tasks remain intrinsically hard, see Section 4.2.

We also now provide a direct link to the Python code used for each model when detailing our experiments in the appendix.

>  Appendix C should explain why the airfoil design space can be modeled as a tuple of 192 two-dimensional control points plus a single scalar for rotation. Where does the training data come from, how is diversity measured, and how does this simplified parameterization affect simulation fidelity and real-world applicability?

We agree this parameterization may not be obvious to non-domain experts. We use a representation based on 192 FFD control point displacements and a scalar angle of attack, following established practices in aerodynamic shape optimization, e.g., [3,4,5]. This approach provides sufficient geometric flexibility to capture a wide range of realistic airfoil shapes and is commonly used in both CFD-based optimization and generative modeling.

As noted in line 690, 1400 configurations/conditions were chosen using Latin hypercube sampling and optimized to generate diverse airfoils, we report the sampled parameter bounds in Table 5. Our training data is sourced from Diniz & Fuge [5], we refer readers to their original paper for full details on data generation.  That being said, it is possible to extend such datasets for even more diversity or better coverage of the configuration space using our Slurm API.

We will revise Appendix C to clarify this information.




> the paper should clarify how Python solver errors are detected across different problems, what typical failure cases look like, and what the observed failure rates are.

We fully agree, and we have designed EngiBench with this robustness in mind. We propose to add the following information to a new appendix section of the paper:

EngiBench is able to handle errors at various levels, while still providing flexibility for advanced usage. The framework includes several mechanisms:
* **Constraints checking:** Each benchmark problem includes standardized checks for constraints and configuration validity (see line 202 and Listing 1, line 13). For example, in the Beams2D problem, setting an invalid volume fraction (e.g., `volfrac = 2.0`) and checking for constraints returns:

`Config.volfrac: 2.0 ∉ [0.0, 1.0] (Theory, error)`

`Config.volfrac: 2.0 ∉ [0.1, 0.9] (Implementation, warning).`

Such pre-simulation checks catch issues before a solver is called. 
* **User control:** While such errors are flagged, users can still choose to simulate invalid designs/configurations—for example, to study failure regions or generate negative data. 
* **Failure tracking:** When solver crashes occur (e.g., due to meshing errors, timeouts, or NaNs), the framework captures and surfaces the exception, even within containers.
* **Failure rates and reporting:** Simulation failure rates vary across tasks and methods. We often track these to compare robustness. For example, the failure ratio for generative airfoil models is reported in Section 4.2.

> More background on the engineering domains and a deeper discussion of robustness would make the work far more accessible—especially to ML researchers with limited domain expertise.

We agree, and we will revise the appendix to include more background information and motivation for each domain. Additionally, we would like to note that the library is currently being used and tested by students at ETH Zurich (it will be used in a course with more than 200 students next Fall semester), and we are actively improving the documentation based on their feedback to make it more accessible and user-friendly for users from various backgrounds. 

Regarding the robustness, we understood it to mean “robustness to errors” (as opposed to robustness to design changes, such as in the “Robust Design” literature) and refer again to the point above.



## Bibliography
[1]: S. Massoudi and J. Schiffmann, “Dimensionless group-driven ensemble neural networks for robust design optimization in engineering,” Journal of Computational Design and Engineering, 2025.

[2] S. Massoudi, C. Bush, and J. Schiffmann, “Robust design optimization of gas-lubricated herringbone grooved journal bearings: Surrogate modeling and experimental validation,” Tribology International, 2025.

[3] Xiaolong He, Jichao Li, Charles A. Mader, Anil Yildirim, and Joaquim R. R. A. Martins. “Robust aerodynamic shape optimization—from a circle to an airfoil.” Aerospace Science and Technology, 2019.

[4] Wei Chen, Kevin Chiu, and Mark Fuge. “Aerodynamic Design Optimization and Shape Exploration using Generative Adversarial Networks.” In AIAA SCITECH Forum. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, 2019.

[5] Cashen Diniz and Mark Fuge. “Optimizing diffusion to diffuse optimal designs.” In AIAA SCITECH Forum. American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, 2024.

We thank the reviewer for their encouraging feedback. We are especially glad they appreciated the API design, cross-domain benchmarking capability, and reproducibility features. Below, we respond to the noted limitations.

> 1. Static, Structured Mesh Only: EngiBench currently supports only static simulations on structured grids. It does not handle unstructured meshes or grammar‑based representations, limiting applicability to certain engineering domains (e.g., complex 3D geometries, assemblies)

This is true, and we mention this in our Limitations section (line 330). We believe that extending EngiBench to support dynamic problems and unstructured meshes should be feasible with the current API and is a natural direction for future work.

> 2. Lack of Dynamic and Multi‐Component Tasks: Real‑world systems often involve dynamic behavior or multi‑part assemblies (e.g., mechanisms, moving parts). The framework does not yet cover time‑varying simulations or joint optimization of interconnected components.

Dynamic and multi-part assemblies are indeed important use-cases (see line 331), but they remain an emerging frontier in ML-driven design. To date, most generative-design research—and even recent advances in single-part topology optimization that use a handful of gradient-descent refinement steps to produce high-fidelity beams [1]—focuses on one-component problems. Multi-body systems introduce extra layers of coupling (contact, kinematics, dynamic loading) that the community is still working on to model effectively. EngiBench/EngiOpt, was built with extensibility in mind: by subclassing our Problem interface and defining its abstract methods (simulate(), optimize(), check_constraints(), etc.), users can plug in multi-part or time-varying simulators and leverage all of our algorithmic and metric infrastructure.

> 3. Benchmark Scale and Diversity: While the set of six core problems is diverse, some industrially relevant domains (e.g., fluid-structure interaction beyond 2D airfoils, battery systems, multiphase flows) remain unexplored. rebuttal.value:
Thank you for the encouraging review. We appreciate your recognition of the integrated real-world simulators, the breadth of compatible methods, and the value of new comparisons (e.g., cross-task) that EngiBench enables. We address the additional questions and concerns below.

> The authors clearly mention their limitations from several perspectives

We agree that our work has certain limitations, which we openly acknowledge. However, we would like to emphasize that these limitations do not undermine the utility of the library. The benchmark problems we include are widely recognized and actively used in the engineering design community. Rather than being fundamental shortcomings, the listed limitations primarily point to natural extensions—many of which are already compatible with our current API—that would enhance the scope of the library in future iterations.

> While the paper mentions distributed computing and high-fidelity simulations, it does not fully discuss the accessibility challenges for smaller labs or individual researchers without large-scale compute clusters or high-performance resources. Even with Docker or Slurm support, running these heavy simulations can be a barrier.

This is a valid and important concern. We specifically kept accessibility in mind when designing the problem set, as we aim for EngiBench to be used not only in research but also in education—we will use EngiBench in a course with over 200 students this Fall at ETH Zurich. Several tasks—such as Beams2D, Photonics2D, and ThermoElasticBeams2D—use lightweight, Python-based simulations that run in seconds on a standard desktop or laptop (see Table 1, “Simu. time” column). These are ideal for teaching, prototyping, and rapid experimentation. 

At the other end of the spectrum, tasks such as Airfoil and HeatConduction3D rely on higher-fidelity simulators and benefit from distributed computing, e.g., via our Slurm API. Including these more demanding problems ensures the benchmark remains relevant for researchers developing methods intended for real-world, high-resolution engineering applications.

This range in simulation complexity is intentional: our goal is to provide a continuum of tasks that can serve both smaller labs with limited resources and large-scale teams who wish to address more complex, difficult, and realistic problems. 

We will clarify this motivation (i.e., how we chose our problem set) more explicitly in the final version.



> The authors show that some generative models struggle (e.g., mode collapse, high simulation failure rates), but they do not explicitly discuss limitations related to how difficult it is to get physically valid and diverse outputs from generative approaches today. This limits practical usage in design exploration.

The difficulty of generating valid and diverse designs is highly problem-dependent. For some tasks (e.g., 2D beams), the design space is relatively well-behaved, while others (e.g., airfoils or power electronics) are far more sensitive to design perturbations or topology. In addition, engineering problems often have hard constraints (e.g., volume fraction or fluid entrapment or connectivity) related to their physical validity or usage that are difficult to capture using ML-based objectives like Mean Squared Error (see line 107 in the paper).

In fact, these challenges are one of our key motivations for releasing EngiBench. A central goal of the benchmark is to make these limitations measurable and comparable across tasks and methods—something that has been missing in prior work. This is also why we explicitly include constraint checks (designed to capture cases where the designs do not meet physical validity checks, such as violating a volume fraction constraint), metrics like the ratio of constraint violations, and diversity (e.g., DPP) as part of the evaluation suite. As far as we are aware, no other benchmarking or evaluation library makes measuring these quantities so straightforward, and helps researchers surface the exact type of limitations that the reviewer has mentioned.

We actually agree with the reviewer regarding the current weaknesses of Generative Models in this domain, which is why we made the library, and will draw out some of these motivating discussion points on existing model weaknesses in a revised discussion section in the final paper. 

> The datasets are based on specific simulation tools and modeling assumptions. The paper does not deeply discuss potential biases introduced by these simulators or whether errors or simplifications in simulation might propagate into ML model evaluations.

This is a fair and important point—simulator assumptions can indeed introduce modeling biases that may propagate to learned models. Quantifying such effects is generally difficult without access to physical experiments, a limitation that affects nearly all simulation-based ML research.

That said, one of the valuable aspects of EngiBench is that it can help bring such issues to light. Because the benchmark spans multiple design problems and simulators—each with their own assumptions and potential quirks—models that exploit artifacts from a particular simulator (e.g., a known bias in a RANS CFD model) are less likely to generalize across all the benchmarks. In this way, cross-problem evaluation acts as a kind of regularization: if a model performs exceptionally well on one task due to simulator-specific shortcuts, its performance should regress toward the mean on other tasks, revealing overfitting to simulation artifacts. In future work, it may even be possible to define different versions of the same design problem backed by different simulators with different fidelities or physical assumptions. Comparing model behavior across such variants could help quantify these biases more systematically.

We will add a brief discussion of this aspect in the Use Cases and Limitations section of the paper. Thank you for the suggestion.

summary.value: EngiBench introduces a badly-needed, open-source benchmark suite for data-driven engineering design, wrapping seven diverse, physics-based design problems (airfoils, heat/elasticity topology optimization, photonics, power-electronics, etc.) into a single, Gym-style Python API that handles simulation calls, constraint checks, datasets, and even adjoint optimizers; its companion library, EngiOpt, provides plug-and-play generative models and surrogate-based optimizers, along with utilities for distributed dataset generation and metrics such as cumulative-optimality gap, diversity, and constraint-violation rates—all of which make cross-domain, reproducible comparisons finally practical and reveal intriguing findings (e.g., vanilla GANs can beat conditional diffusion on some constrained tasks, while circuit surrogates remain brittle).

strengths_contributions.value:
Primary contributions:
-- Breadth of curated problems & datasets – Seven rigorously packaged design tasks spanning fluids, heat, EM, structures, and circuits—each with ready-to-use datasets and Docker/Slurm-friendly simulators. As well as unified, versioned API – A Gym-style interface that standardizes design variables, conditions, objectives, constraint checks, simulation calls, and rendering across domains. Swapping problems is often a one-line change.
-- Companion algorithm zoo (EngiOpt) – CleanRL-style implementations of GANs, conditional GANs, diffusion models, Bayesian optimization, etc., wired to EngiBench for out-of-the-box benchmarking. The benchmark also offer metrics for distributed dataset generation, feasibility diagnostics, metric computation (MMD, diversity, cumulative-optimality-gap, constraint-violation rates), and adjoint refinement.
-- Initial experiments show how the framework enables fair, multi-metric comparisons; e.g., unconditioned GANs sometimes outperform conditional diffusion on certain constrained tasks, and surrogate models can struggle on stiff circuit problems.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
--Although the proof-of-concept experiments help validate the benchmark, the discussion of the ML-based methods is still too thin. For example, Appendix C should explain why the airfoil design space can be modeled as a tuple of 192 two-dimensional control points plus a single scalar for rotation. Where does the training data come from, how is diversity measured, and how does this simplified parameterization affect simulation fidelity and real-world applicability? 
--In addition, while the library provides an easy-to-use API, the paper should clarify how Python solver errors are detected across different problems, what typical failure cases look like, and what the observed failure rates are. More background on the engineering domains and a deeper discussion of robustness would make the work far more accessible—especially to ML researchers with limited domain expertise.

summary.value: This paper introduces an open-source framework for data-driven engineering design. Traditional engineering design relies heavily on expensive physics-based simulations and requires deep domain expertise, which makes it slow and hard to scale. EngiBench addresses this by providing a unified API, a collection of diverse real-world engineering design problems (like airfoil shapes, heat conduction, photonics), and a companion library (EngiOpt) with various ML and optimization algorithms. The authors demonstrate that EngiBench makes it easy to test and compare algorithms across different design tasks.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. EngiBench includes many challenging engineering problems (like airfoils, heat conduction, and photonics), each using real physics simulators. This makes it a much more realistic and meaningful testbed compared to simplified or purely synthetic benchmarks.

2. The framework supports many ML methods, such as surrogate-based optimization, inverse design, and both conditional and unconditional generative models (like GANs, diffusion models, and BézierGANs). This allows fair and direct comparison of very different approaches under the same setup, which is rare in other benchmarks.

3. EngiBench introduces engineering-specific metrics, like cumulative optimality gap (COG), ratio of constraint violations (RVC), maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and determinantal point process (DPP) scores for diversity. These give a more complete picture of model performance and encourage development of models that work well in real engineering tasks.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The authors clearly mention their limitations from several perspectives: (1) Representation: They do not yet support unstructured meshes or grammar-based design representations. (2) Simulation type: Their benchmarks focus on static simulations only, while many real-world systems are dynamic and involve motion or changing shapes. (3) System complexity: They do not include multi-part or assembly-level tasks, such as optimizing multiple interdependent components together.

Additionally, I have the following questions and concerns:
1. While the paper mentions distributed computing and high-fidelity simulations, it does not fully discuss the accessibility challenges for smaller labs or individual researchers without large-scale compute clusters or high-performance resources. Even with Docker or Slurm support, running these heavy simulations can be a barrier.

2. The authors show that some generative models struggle (e.g., mode collapse, high simulation failure rates), but they do not explicitly discuss limitations related to how difficult it is to get physically valid and diverse outputs from generative approaches today. This limits practical usage in design exploration.

3. The datasets are based on specific simulation tools and modeling assumptions. The paper does not deeply discuss potential biases introduced by these simulators or whether errors or simplifications in simulation might propagate into ML model evaluations.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Code and data is available in supplementary materials, and I confirm I have taken a glance.

final_justification.value:
After reading the authors' rebuttal, I am satisfied with their responses and have decided to raise my score. The authors addressed my key concerns with detailed clarifications and thoughtful revisions planned for the final version. Specifically:

 - **Accessibility and computational cost**: The authors clarified that the benchmark includes a spectrum of tasks, many of which are lightweight and runnable on standard hardware, making the suite accessible to smaller labs. This resolves my concern about high compute requirements limiting usability.

 - **Design challenge diversity and generative model evaluation**: The authors provided a compelling justification for including tasks with varying difficulty and design constraints. Their discussion of physical validity checks and diversity metrics demonstrates awareness of evaluation limitations and offers a principled way to capture failure cases in generative models.

 - **Simulator assumptions and potential biases**: While the paper does not fully quantify simulator-induced bias, the authors acknowledged this issue and articulated how EngiBench helps surface such biases by spanning multiple simulators. I find this explanation reasonable and see the current framing as a good first step.

Overall, I believe the paper offers a valuable benchmark suite and motivates meaningful future research. The authors have shown clear intent to improve clarity and transparency in the final version. No major unresolved concerns remain.

summary.value: This work introduces **EngiBench**, an open‑source framework and dataset library for data‑driven engineering design, along with EngiOpt, a companion toolkit of ML and optimization algorithms compatible with EngiBench’s API. EngiBench unifies diverse physics‑based simulation problems (aerodynamics, heat conduction, photonics, power electronics, etc.) under a standardized Python interface, provides versioned datasets, constraint‐checking utilities, and easy deployment via containerization. EngiOpt offers implementations of baseline methods—GANs, conditional GANs, diffusion models, surrogate‐based optimizers—and demonstrates cross‐domain evaluation through proof‑of‑concept experiments, revealing nontrivial challenges in constrained design spaces

strengths_contributions.value:
**1. Unified, Extensible API**: A well‑designed Python interface abstracts away simulation complexity, enabling rapid prototyping of inverse design, surrogate modeling, and gradient‑based optimization across multiple domains.

**2. Diverse, Versioned Benchmarks**: EngiBench includes a curated suite of real‑world problems (airfoils, topology optimization in 2D/3D, thermoelastic beams, photonics, power electronics) with publicly available datasets and simulators. Each problem is versioned to ensure reproducibility.

**3. Cross‐Domain Benchmarking Capability**: Through EngiOpt, the authors demonstrate that comparing generative and surrogate methods across multiple problems is straightforward—simply switching a problem_id. Their experiments reveal surprising insights (e.g., unconditional GANs outperform conditional diffusion on some metrics) and underscore the sensitivity of design manifolds. 

**4. Reproducibility and Usability Features**: Built‑in constraint checking, containerized environments (Docker/Podman/Apptainer), integration with HuggingFace Datasets, PyTorch, BoTorch, Pymoo, and support for distributed execution lower the barrier for both ML and engineering researchers to adopt the framework.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**1. Static, Structured Mesh Only**: EngiBench currently supports only static simulations on structured grids. It does not handle unstructured meshes or grammar‑based representations, limiting applicability to certain engineering domains (e.g., complex 3D geometries, assemblies).

**2. Lack of Dynamic and Multi‐Component Tasks**:
Real‑world systems often involve dynamic behavior or multi‑part assemblies (e.g., mechanisms, moving parts). The framework does not yet cover time‑varying simulations or joint optimization of interconnected components.

**3. Benchmark Scale and Diversity**: While the set of six core problems is diverse, some industrially relevant domains (e.g., fluid-structure interaction beyond 2D airfoils, battery systems, multiphase flows) remain unexplored. Future extensions are needed to test ML methods under even broader physics scenarios.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: This work presents EngiBench and EngiOpt, a unified, open-source framework and toolkit that enable standardized benchmarking and algorithm development across diverse physics-based engineering design problems. With its extensible API, versioned datasets, and strong focus on reproducibility, the paper provides valuable resources and insights that advance data-driven engineering design research. I believe this submission meets the acceptance criteria.

summary.value: The paper introduces a collection of benchmark problems for machine learning in application to engineering design. The accompanying library includes a number of common design problems and cleanly wraps third party simulators, making it near effortless for practitioners to evaluate models trained for these tasks, or to create custom datasets for these tasks. The paper also provides a collection of models trained on these tasks, providing a clear baseline for future research to improve on.

strengths_contributions.value:
The paper is written well and makes its contributions clear. It was enjoyable to read and I commend the authors on their work putting together the EngiBench library and rigorously benchmarking various models.
This paper addresses a significant gap in the field of ML for engineering design, namely a standardized set of benchmark problems and associated metrics. The EngiBench library can potentially fill the same roll in engineering design as gym(nasium) does in reinforcement learning, and I would very much like to see its adoption grow. Just as gymnasium has enabled significant strides in research on RL algorithms, EngiBench may well be an enabling factor for significant research progress in ML for engineering design.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
There are a few points which would make the paper stronger if properly addressed, in particular
 - The paper does not provide justification for the specific problems chosen. These problems do cover a number of domains, which is good, but some discussion could be added about the significance of the problems.
 - The benchmark problems seem to be quite specific in terms of actual configuration, and it would be nice to see more flexible configurations of these problems, for example in the heat conduction problem, one can imagine a user being able to specify multiple heat sources or sinks. Similarly multiple circuit configurations and topologies in the power electronics case would be a valuable addition. Adding some configuration options like this would mean that the problems would be representative of a larger range of real world problems. 
 - One important aspect of a library like this is the possibility of users contributing new problems or more complex configurations of problems. As these contributions grow, so will the value of these benchmarks and this library. However extending the library with new problems doesn't seem to be discussed in the paper. I noticed there is some information about this in the documentation, though it may be good to include something in the paper on this point.

Some minor points:
 - the order of the individual metrics is unclear in table 2 (should I read left to right or top to bottom?). Please clarify this, and also add an explanation for why one value (is it RVC?) is always NA in the photonics problem.
 - on line 126 the COG is defined using $(\tilde{f}-f^\star)$ which is negative when $f^\star$ is defined as a maximum (on line 123). Most of the problems are defined as minimization problems, in which case this makes sense, but is probably the wrong way around here.
 - the indices on line 130 aren't quite right. j has been introduced twice, and I suspect something like $g_i(x_j)$ was intended.
 - some words on the quality of the optimizer in the paragraph starting on line 212. How close should we expect the optimization result to be compared to the global optimum?
 - line 231 uses a capital C for the first "conduction" and lower case for the second.

dataset_code_comments.value: All code is available on github and has a clean interface, making it easy to use. Documentation is hosted online with example usage and clear instructions for generating custom datasets. The baseline models and training code is also easily accessible on github.

additional_feedback.value: It looks like some of the datasets hosted on huggingface are quite small (almost all less than 5k examples, some with only 400). This is not necessarily a problem as one can relatively easily generate more data themselves, but it is always good to have more diversity in a dataset.

final_justification.value: The paper is well written and addresses an important topic. The authors have fixed any minor errors and added clarifications where needed. I therefore recommend this paper is accepted for publication.

title.value: EngiBench: A Framework for Data-Driven Engineering Design Research

TLDR.value: A novel suite benchmark problems for data-driven engineering design (beams, airfoils, heat conduction, etc.) under a standardized API.

abstract.value: Engineering design optimization seeks to automatically determine the shapes, topologies, or parameters of components that maximize performance under given conditions. This process often depends on physics-based simulations, which are difficult to install, computationally expensive, and require domain-specific expertise. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce EngiBench, the first open‐source library and datasets spanning diverse domains for data‐driven engineering design. EngiBench provides a unified API and a curated set of benchmarks---covering aeronautics, heat conduction, photonics, and more---that enable fair, reproducible comparisons of optimization and machine learning algorithms, such as generative or surrogate models. We also release EngiOpt, a companion library offering a collection of such algorithms compatible with the EngiBench interface. Both libraries are modular, letting users plug in novel algorithms or problems, automate end-to-end experiment workflows, and leverage built-in utilities for visualization, dataset generation, feasibility checks, and performance analysis. We demonstrate their versatility through experiments comparing state-of-the-art techniques across multiple engineering design problems, an undertaking that was previously prohibitively time-consuming to perform. Finally, we show that these problems pose significant challenges for standard machine learning methods due to highly sensitive and constrained design manifolds.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15).

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.
